title: Prototype to demo in a year: 15,000+ prompts, ~500K lines of C#, zero written by hand, after 15+ years of writing code myself
author: devtainer
selftext:
Hi AI game devers!

I've been doing gamedev as a hobby for around 10 years, and I'm finally getting to my first ever Steam demo! This video is one year of development squeezed into one minute.

The game was fully vibecoded (Claude Code and Codex), but it wasn't an easy ride. I'm a software developer with 15+ years of experience. AI can do complex things very fast and save you a ton of time, but it still needs to be guided by experience and good planning.

Some tips I came up with during development:

\- Define future goals upfront. I'm planning a local co-op mode, so it's written in the rules and every feature is built with that in mind. Will save a lot of time once I will switch to this task!

\- Build core systems early. I didn't have all languages from day 1, but right after prototyping I made a system for quick language integration. Every line in the game has a key and is never hardcoded in code or UI.

\- Keep an index of your systems. Once the codebase grows, AI starts losing track of it and reinvents things instead of reusing what already exists. Make a separate index for mid-big features and push AI to read it before any change. Keep it short.

\- Keep a list of repeated mistakes. If AI makes the same mistake again and again, write it down and add a rule to check that list before any change. This helped me a lot to stop going in circles. Keep it short.

\- Use your voice. Maybe it's obvious now, but it wasn't for me at first. You speak much faster than you type, so AI gets more context. Make sure you have good voice recognition.

\- Ask for tests with every feature and every bug fix. AI breaks old things without noticing. Tests catch it before you do. A quarter of my code is tests and I don't regret a single line.

\- Fix the cause, not the symptom. AI loves to drop a quick patch right where the bug shows up. Make it find the root cause first, otherwise patches pile up and start fighting each other.

\- Make it show you. Review and read everything carefully! Some people ignore outputs or even checks of what id did. Sometimes it's just enough to read text carefull to see what AI did wrong, sometimes video/screenshot. Saves a lot of back and forth.

\- Keep tunable values out of code. All balance numbers live in config files, and AI built me simple HTML editors for them. I tweak balance with sliders, no prompts needed.

\- Run agents in parallel. I have several copies of the project, each agent works in its own, and a shared task board keeps them from stepping on each other.



Hope it's helpful! Happy to answer questions in the comments.

Would really appreciate it if [you wishlist game on Steam ](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5116620/Grumpy_Hero_Grinder?utm_source=reddit)

Thanks for reading!

comments.author: Fit_Eye_3564
comments.body: Could really speed up or cut some of the fluff from the rough beginnings, it really didnt keep me wanting to watch the video. But the game looks solid. Just wish it focused more on the finished product, especially since it looks like you want us to try buy or wishlist your game.

replies.author: devtainer
replies.body: Hi mate, thank you for a feedback I really appreciate that! Would you mind to be a little more specific - which exact timing are you talking about? may be in days like 1-50 or in seconds of the video, would be really happy to know, thanks!

replies.author: cafeblake
replies.body: no way, i loved it, i love seeing the potato version evolve, anyone actually doing dev appreciates that

replies.author: devtainer
replies.body: great that you loved this and thanks :) Its a good point though that for people who are not into gamedev dev it might be a bit boring, so I do really wonder how to make it more catchy for them as I am trying to market also with gaming auditory

replies.author: cafeblake
replies.body:
Non devs just wanna see the final product to know if they want to play it, so for that you just need to market it like a normal game imo.

For vibe coders they want to know they don’t have to actually do work to make millions, so you won’t satisfy them unless it’s shiny and polished and you give them the magic incantation to make money with no effort.

For anyone trying to actually make something with feeling they’ll appreciate that look back and the history. 

Different targets, different requirements

comments.author: IriFlina
comments.body: One thing I’ve found is if you’re early on in the prototyping phase, trying to make your core gameplay idea/loop fun do NOT make the ai write tests. It just slows the process down when you’re trying to see if you can even make the game fun or not.

replies.author: devtainer
replies.body: it's actually a really good point, agree!

comments.author: aj_marshall
comments.body: This is how AI game development should be. 10/10.

comments.author: No_Butterfly_2908
comments.body:
Curious about this. I’ve also been an indie developer for a while and work in Enterprise software as a consultant, so don’t really have a lot of free time (young family to boot). I’ve been exploring AI game dev for some time now - but how much does something like this cost? I built a prototype of something today, using the free Fable windows and resets and it basically used 3 five hour windows on 5.2 @ Medium over the course of a couple of hours - my approach was similar to yours, show me, tell me, generate visuals of architecture and update your rules etc. 

I can’t see doing *anything* like this without a wad of money. 

Did you do anything yourself to save on cost? Assets, for example?

replies.author: FordEngineerman
replies.body:
The $20 and $100 subscriptions are surprisingly generous especially if you are careful to use the correct models and effort levels for the scope of the task. They cost like 1/10th of what usage credits do.

I'm on the $20 tier and as long as I stick to Opus 5.5 Medium effort or lower I can work for 5-10 hours a week pretty easily without hitting a usage limit. If I want to really focus for a week then I try to use Sonnet for more rote implementation tasks and its practically free to run by comparison to Opus. I could work with Sonnet for probably 100+ hours a week without running out of budget if I didn't mind having to fix some of the code or be much more precise with prompting.

replies.author: devtainer
replies.body:
I would say most valuable is a time :) I spent a lot of time on it.

Money wise it's approx 400$ / month including asset packs and different models I used.

Don't use fable as your default it is very expensive, start with opus 5.5 high-xhigh. Generation isn't that expensive if you use popular 3d generation solutions on the market (don't want to ad concrete, it's easy to find). Let your local model to call those solutions API to generate 3d, it costs like nothing. Also consider asset packs, I've purchased many of those, they are still quite cheap.
